name: Aaron Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential; I want both what you'd say publicly and what you think privately. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Aaron, 27, and I lead the billing software team at a tech company. My master's helped me learn the design, but the work I enjoy is tracing a disputed receipt back through three old systems and teaching a junior developer why the number changed. I don't use AI tools, and I get tired of meetings where someone with a slide says the receipts will check themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team a script that sorts routine bug reports is fine, as long as a developer still reads the report. I don't use AI tools myself; I know our billing system well enough to find a fault without a machine guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job feels fairly steady if little changes. I lead the billing team, earn around the normal rate and have roughly three months of expenses in the bank, though the renewal on my flat could eat some of that. A few other firms are within commuting range, but I would rather keep this team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on reviewing billing fixes and training the new developer at the desk beside mine. In the first year I'd ask for the usual pay review and keep putting 150 aside each month if the rent allows it; I wouldn't buy a tool just because a vendor called.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with the flat renewal in the back of my mind. Small software changes are normal; we've been through them before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the new developer catch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The new developer, Leila, caught a rounding error last week because she checked a receipt by hand. I don't want a sorting script to send that kind of report to the wrong pile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When will you know whether you can keep saving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rent notice comes in February, so the savings amount depends on that figure. If the increase is large, I'll keep the monthly transfer smaller rather than run down the account.

say: I'd accept a **bug sorter** if someone still reads billing reports.
I'd say **hand checks** still catch errors in customer receipts.
think: I feel fairly secure with **three months saved** and some nearby firms.
I worry about the **February rent renewal** more than small AI tools.
do: Keep reviewing **billing fixes** and coaching the new developer.
Ask for the **usual pay review** in the first year.
Save **150 monthly** if the February rent allows it.
feel: **Calm** about work, with rent renewal on my mind.
S0.quote: I know our billing system well enough to find a fault without a machine guessing.
fieldNote: **Billing knowledge** and a three-month cushion support job confidence, though rent may erode savings.
He refuses AI personally, yet accepts a **sorting script** if people still read and verify customer reports.

steps.text: Review billing fixes and coach the new developer
Save 150 monthly if February rent allows it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company should tell us which coding and checking tasks are changing, not just put up a screen showing faster output. AI taking writing, planning and customer replies would touch almost everything my team does before any robot enters an office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If management can get acceptable fixes without paying for a full billing team, my lead title may buy time but not safety. I don't use these tools, and I'd be slower than my colleagues to learn them; if February rent rises, three months saved could go quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager for a written plan showing which releases still need people, then continue leading the current billing cycle. If the company runs a tool trial in the first year, I'd inspect the customer receipts and log every mismatch, but I would not operate the AI myself until its errors are understood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can do the checking, yet I might be training a system that makes my team smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would handle the trial first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leila, the junior developer, would probably be asked to check the output first because she is keen on new tools. I'd ask her to bring me three actual receipts where the tool was wrong, not a slide about average speed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say if the error log were hidden?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the same thing in the team meeting: publish the mismatch log. If management hid the errors, I would refuse to sign the release, even if that cost me the lead role.

say: I'd ask for a **written task plan** before billing work moves to AI.
I'd demand an open **mismatch log** before signing a release.
think: I may lose **team members** and eventually my own lead pay.
I would learn more slowly than colleagues who use AI; a **February rent rise** could shrink my cushion.
do: Request a **written release plan** from my manager now.
Keep leading the **billing cycle** in the first year.
Inspect **customer receipts** and record trial mismatches before signing releases.
feel: **Anxious** about team size and my slower start with tools.
S1.quote: I might be training a system that makes my team smaller.
fieldNote: **Coding and checking** sit at the center of his work, so steady change puts his own income at risk.
He resists tool use but offers to inspect **real receipts** and would withhold his signature if errors were hidden.

steps.text: Keep leading the billing release cycle while tools are tested
Inspect customer receipts and record mismatches in the tool trial

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell people full thinking AI by 2028 reaches billing code at once; robots arriving around 2031 have little to do with my desk. The company owes workers plain numbers about paid posts, not speeches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my billing job could disappear within a year of that system, and I haven't used the tools that might be left to supervise. Three months of savings is some time, not a new trade. A higher February rent could shorten it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check the February lease terms before committing to another year and ask my brother what a room in his house would cost if I lost my job. If I were cut in the first year after 2028, I'd apply to paid billing support posts at the two nearby firms and move to his room only if the terms worked; I would not quit now on a forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I would still go to work tomorrow, but I'd be adding up the rent and wondering whether my skill has an employer left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has your brother offered that room?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother has a spare room, but he has not offered it. I'd ask him directly and pay a share of the bills if he agrees; I would not just appear at his door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What wage would make the support work possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A support post would need to cover rent and bills. I won't take a new title with half the wage just to say I stayed in software.

say: I'd say **2028 thinking AI** reaches billing code before 2031 robots matter.
I'd ask employers for **plain paid-post numbers**.
think: I could lose my **billing lead job** quickly after 2028.
My **three-month cushion** could shrink if February rent rises.
do: Check the **February lease** before renewing now.
Ask my **brother's room terms** before counting on family help.
After a cut, apply to **paid billing support** only if wages cover bills.
feel: **Alarmed** about losing a specialised job with a short cushion.
S2.quote: Three months of savings is some time, not a new trade.
fieldNote: **2028 thinking AI** targets billing code directly, and later robots do not delay the threat.
His brother's room is **unoffered**, so he would ask and pay bills rather than treating family housing as guaranteed.

steps.text: Ask brother now about a paid room if billing job ends
Apply to nearby billing support posts only if pay covers bills
Move to brother's room after a cut only if he agrees on terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years before 2031 gives our team time to show what billing mistakes a system still makes. The robots come around 2034, but the thinking system reaches our code first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still wouldn't rush into AI tools, but I could learn the parts needed to audit a release if a trusted colleague showed me working examples. I may be less suited to that than Leila, so I would also explore the paid billing support work at other firms before I need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Leila to walk me through one AI-assisted billing fix each month, using test accounts, and I'd practice checking its receipts myself. I'd also put 150 into savings when rent permits; in the first year after 2031, I'd apply for human billing review posts only if those posts exist and the pay covers housing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the five years give me a slower way to learn. I don't have to claim I'm suddenly a fan of the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why use test accounts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A test account cannot send a wrong bill to a real customer. I could make mistakes while I learn there, and Leila can tell me what I missed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask another firm about review work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the other firms whether a reviewer signs the final bill and what that job pays. If their answer is only a job title, I will keep looking.

say: I'd say **2031 thinking AI** reaches billing before 2034 robots.
I'd ask for **real error examples** while we still have years to prepare.
think: I could learn **release auditing** slowly with a trusted colleague and safe examples.
I may need **paid billing review** elsewhere if my team shrinks.
do: Practice one **AI-assisted billing fix** monthly with Leila on test accounts.
Save **150 monthly** when the new rent allows it.
After 2031, seek **paid review posts** only where wages cover housing.
feel: **Anxious**, but relieved to have years for a measured trial.
S3.quote: A test account cannot send a wrong bill to a real customer.
fieldNote: **Five years** make limited AI learning plausible despite his resistant habits and lack of current use.
He ties any move to **real review wages** and uses test accounts to protect customer bills while learning.

steps.text: Practice checking one AI-assisted billing fix monthly on test accounts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade before 2036 is time to teach younger developers the billing rules and learn what replaces the routine code. Robots around 2039 still come after thinking AI has changed software work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 37, perhaps in a review role or perhaps out of software. Ten years makes the shift less abrupt, but my flat rent is due next spring and I still have to keep saving while I work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the billing handbook up to date and teach the next junior developer how to trace a disputed receipt. If the February rent is manageable, I'd save toward six months of expenses, then pay for an evening electrical repair course only if fees fit my savings and I can verify local apprenticeships; in the first year after 2036 I'd compare paid billing review with repair openings and move only for work that covers my bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the long future, though calm enough to do my present work. I wouldn't borrow money for a course on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What belongs in that handbook?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The handbook would show the rounding error Leila found and the steps to reproduce it. A future reviewer should be able to challenge a machine's answer with a real receipt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a repair course worth taking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask repair shops what an apprentice earns before paying course fees. My father learned by working beside someone; I would want the same practical chance, not a certificate with no job behind it.

say: I'd say **2036 thinking AI** changes billing before 2039 robots arrive.
I'd tell junior developers to learn **billing rules** and keep worked examples.
think: I could find **review work** at 37, but I cannot count on it.
I still face the **February rent** and need to build savings now.
do: Keep the **billing handbook** current and teach disputed-receipt checks.
Save toward **six months' expenses** if rent permits.
Check **apprentice wages**, then pay for an affordable course only with verified openings; later switch only if wages cover bills.
feel: **Uneasy** about later pay, though able to work and save now.
S4.quote: A future reviewer should be able to challenge a machine's answer with a real receipt.
fieldNote: **Ten years** ease the timing, but current rent still controls what he can save and study.
His repair course depends on **verified local apprenticeships** and fees his savings can cover without borrowing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I could lose my billing job before I can build a bigger cushion. Honest numbers on paid posts, a clear notice period and affordable training with practical work attached would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what happens when a customer disputes a machine-made bill. Someone has to listen, trace the mistake and sign the correction; I'd like employers to say who that person is and what they earn.

headlineQuote: Someone has to listen, trace the mistake and sign the correction; I'd like employers to say who that person is and what they earn.
portrait: Aaron is a **27-year-old billing software lead** with a master's degree and strong skill in tracing disputed receipts.
He earns **typical pay**, has about three months saved and faces a February rent renewal, with some nearby software firms.
He avoids AI tools, trusts **hand checks**, and remains uneasy about rent even in AI Plateau.
Steady disruption threatens **billing jobs**; 2028 AGI alarms him because thinking AI reaches code before robots matter.
More time lets him **learn cautiously** on test accounts, save if rent allows and consider repair training only with verified apprenticeships.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase his billing role before he builds a larger cushion.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid-post numbers**, clear notice and affordable training tied to practical work would help him respond.
